# Is non-realizability at (4,9) generated by minors?

Written 2026-08-01. Companion to `ai/omreal/WALK_THEORY.md` (the walk) and
`ai/omreal/SCOPING.md` (the measurements). This file asks whether the
extensional sweep can be turned into a classification theorem, measures the
answer, and says plainly what the answer is worth.

**Short answer.** Mostly, but not enough to be a theorem worth the name.
**91.1%** of the certified non-realizable uniform rank-4 classes on 9
elements contain one of the 24 non-realizable (4,8) classes as a
single-element deletion. Contractions never witness anything, and we verify
why. The other **8.9%** are minor-minimal — genuinely new 9-element
obstructions — and there are **1,279 of them in the prefix measured**, on
track for order 10^4 catalogue-wide. So a finite excluded-minor statement
exists at n ≤ 9, but at n = 9 it degenerates into a table of tens of
thousands of entries with no visible common structure. The honest
deliverable is the closure fraction, the mechanism behind it, and one
proposition that sharpens an open conjecture — not a classification.

---

## 1. Conventions

Ground set E = {1..n}; bases are r-subsets in **colex** order; a uniform
chirotope is an alternating χ: E^r → {±1} satisfying the three-term
Grassmann–Plücker conditions; a **class** is an orbit under
G' = S_n × {0,1}^n × {0,1} (relabel, reorient, global sign). These are
`ai/omgamma/OMGAMMA.md` §2 verbatim, and the canonical key is the one
`coverage_checker.canonical_convention` documents. Catalogs used:

| cell | classes | non-realizable | certificates |
|---|---|---|---|
| (4,5) | 1 | 0 | `data/certs_4_5.jsonl` (this work) |
| (4,6) | 1 | 0 | `data/certs_4_6.jsonl` (this work) |
| (4,7) | 11 | 0 | `data/certs_4_7.jsonl` (this work) |
| (4,8) | 2,628 | **24** | `ai/omreal/certs_4_8.jsonl` |
| (4,9) | 9,276,595 | sweep in progress | `ai/omreal/sweep_state/certs/` |
| (3,7) | 11 | 0 | `data/certs_3_7.jsonl` (this work) |
| (3,8) | 135 | **0** | `ai/omreal/certs_3_8.jsonl` |
| (3,9) | 4,382 | 1 (non-Pappus) | `ai/omreal/certs_3_9.jsonl` |
| (3,10) | 312,356 | 242 | `ai/omreal/certs_3_10_nonrealizable.jsonl` |

The (4,5), (4,6), (4,7) and (3,7) rows are new here: they were needed for
the minor-minimality claim at n = 8 (§3) and did not exist. All 1 + 1 + 11 +
11 = 24 of those certificates were produced with `ai/omreal/realize.py` and
accepted by `checkcert.py` (`cert47.py`).

## 2. The lemmas

Everything in this section is standard; it is written out because the rest
of the document is machine-checked and the lemmas should not be the weak
link. For definitions of deletion and contraction of an oriented matroid see
[BLSWZ] (Björner, Las Vergnas, Sturmfels, White, Ziegler, *Oriented
Matroids*, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press 1999); we do not cite
proposition numbers because the text was not consulted directly, and the
proofs below are complete in themselves.

**Definition.** For a uniform rank-r chirotope χ on E and e ∈ E:
* the **deletion** χ∖e is the rank-r chirotope on E∖{e} given by
  (χ∖e)(B) = χ(B) for every r-subset B ⊆ E∖{e};
* the **contraction** χ/e is the rank-(r−1) chirotope on E∖{e} given by
  (χ/e)(x₁..x_{r−1}) = χ(e, x₁..x_{r−1}).

Both are again **uniform**: every basis of the minor is a basis of χ, and χ
never vanishes. Both are again **chirotopes**: the three-term GP conditions
of χ∖e are literally a subset of those of χ, and those of χ/e are the
subset of χ's whose index set L contains e.

> **Lemma D (deletion preserves realizability).** If χ is realized by a
> configuration X = (x₁..x_n) in R^r — meaning χ(B) = sign det X_B for every
> basis B — then χ∖e is realized by the subconfiguration (x_i)_{i≠e}.
>
> *Proof.* Every bracket of the subconfiguration is literally a bracket of X.
> ∎
>
> **Contrapositive, the form used here:** if χ∖e is non-realizable for some
> e, then χ is non-realizable.

> **Lemma C (contraction preserves realizability).** If χ is realized by X
> then χ/e is realized by the images of (x_i)_{i≠e} under the quotient
> π: R^r → R^r/⟨x_e⟩ ≅ R^{r−1}, up to one global sign.
>
> *Proof.* Choose a basis of R^r whose first vector is x_e. In that basis
> det(x_e, x_{i₁}..x_{i_{r−1}}) = c · det'(π x_{i₁} .. π x_{i_{r−1}}) with c
> a nonzero constant independent of the i's. So the two sign vectors agree
> if c > 0 and are opposite if c < 0, and χ and −χ are the same oriented
> matroid. ∎

Both were checked computationally on a real certificate, in exact integer /
rational arithmetic: for a realized (4,9) class, all 9 column-restricted
sub-matrices reproduce the 9 deletions bracket for bracket, and all 9
projections reproduce the 9 contractions up to global sign
(`minorlib.py` header test; re-runnable).

> **Lemma M (single-element minors suffice).** If every single-element minor
> of a uniform OM χ is realizable, then every proper minor of χ is
> realizable.
>
> *Proof.* A proper minor is χ∖A/B with A, B disjoint and A ∪ B ≠ ∅. Pick
> e ∈ A ∪ B; then χ∖A/B is a minor of N, where N = χ∖e if e ∈ A and N = χ/e
> if e ∈ B. N is realizable by hypothesis, and realizability is minor-closed
> by Lemmas D and C applied repeatedly to N. ∎

So a class is **minor-minimal non-realizable** exactly when it is
non-realizable and all of its single-element minors are realizable. That is
the property measured below.

> **Lemma K (contractions cannot witness at (4,9)).** For a uniform rank-4
> chirotope on 9 elements, χ/e is a uniform rank-3 chirotope on 8 elements.
> Every one of the 135 such classes is realizable.
>
> *Verification, not assumption.* `ai/omreal/certs_3_8.jsonl` holds 135
> records, one per class of the complete (3,8) catalog, each an explicit
> integer 3×8 matrix; `checkcert.py` accepts all 135 and reports
> `NON_REALIZABLE 0`. Independently, all 185,139 contractions computed in
> this work canonicalize into that catalog and none lands on a
> non-realizable row (there are none to land on).

The same argument one rank down (Lemma K for (3,10)): contractions of a
rank-3 OM on 10 elements have rank 2 on 9 elements, where there is exactly
one uniform class for every n (`OMGAMMA.md` §5, "r = 2") and it is realized
by any convex polygon.

---

## 3. What a classification theorem here can and cannot be

Let N₉ denote the set of minor-minimal non-realizable classes in U(4,9).
Then:

> **Theorem (n ≤ 9, rank 4).** A uniform rank-4 oriented matroid on n ≤ 9
> elements is non-realizable **iff** it has a minor isomorphic to one of the
> 24 non-realizable (4,8) classes or to a member of N₉.

*Proof.* (⇐) is Lemmas D and C applied repeatedly along the minor, plus the
fact that the 24 and the members of N₉ are non-realizable, which is
certified. (⇒): for n ≤ 7 there is nothing to prove — the 1 class at (4,4)
(the identity matrix realizes it), and the 1 + 1 + 11 classes at (4,5),
(4,6), (4,7), are all certified realizable. At n = 8 the non-realizable
classes are exactly the 24, and they are themselves minor-minimal: by Lemma
M it is enough that their single-element minors are realizable, and those
are (4,7) deletions and (3,7) contractions, all 11 + 11 of which are
certified realizable here. At n = 9, a non-realizable class either has a
non-realizable single-element minor — necessarily a deletion, by Lemma K,
and necessarily one of the 24, because (4,8) is completely classified — or
it does not, in which case Lemma M makes it minor-minimal, so it lies in N₉
by definition. ∎

**This is honest but nearly vacuous, and the reason should be stated up
front.** At n = 9 the (⇒) direction is a tautology once N₉ is *defined* as
the minor-minimal set. The theorem has content only to the extent that

1. **N₉ is small** relative to the non-realizable population — the closure
   fraction (§4); and
2. **N₉ is describable** — a family, a template, something other than a
   list (§7).

(1) holds moderately: 91.1%. (2) does **not** hold, as far as this work can
see. So what follows should be read as a measurement, not a classification.

---

## 4. The closure fraction

For each certified non-realizable (4,9) class, all nine deletions were
computed, canonicalized, and identified against the (4,8) catalog; likewise
all nine contractions against the (3,8) catalog.

### 4.1 The two corpora

| corpus | non-realizable classes | with ≥1 non-realizable **deletion** | fraction | 95% Wilson |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| sweep prefix (depth-ordered, 15.58% of the catalog) | 14,396 | 13,117 | **91.12%** | [90.64%, 91.57%] |
| uniform random sample over all 9,276,595 classes | 116 | 105 | **90.52%** | [83.81%, 94.62%] |

**With ≥1 non-realizable contraction: 0 of 20,571 classes tested** (14,512
of them non-realizable), across both corpora. What is actually checked is
that all 185,139 contractions are valid rank-3 chirotopes on 8 elements and
that every one canonicalizes into the complete 135-class (3,8) catalog —
whose members are, all 135 of them, certified realizable. Lemma K,
confirmed extensionally rather than assumed.

Number of non-realizable deletions per class (sweep prefix):

| # non-realizable deletions | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| classes | **1,279** | 10,021 | 2,703 | 393 |

All 24 of the (4,8) obstructions occur as a witness (21 of 24 in the much
smaller uniform corpus), with a very skewed frequency: the top four
(`cat_4_8` rows 2330, 2146, 2611, 2391) supply 10,432 of the 16,606 witness
occurrences (62.8%), while row 2597 occurs once. So the obstruction set is
used very unevenly, but none of it is redundant.

### 4.2 Is the depth-ordered prefix biased?

| tree depth | non-realizable | with a witness | fraction |
|---|---|---|---|
| ≤ 10 | 45 | 45 | 100.00% |
| 11 | 107 | 106 | 99.07% |
| 12 | 319 | 308 | 96.55% |
| 13 | 898 | 848 | 94.43% |
| 14 | 2,304 | 2,124 | 92.19% |
| 15 | 5,423 | 4,915 | 90.63% |
| 16 | 5,300 | 4,771 | 90.02% |

The fraction **falls with depth and then flattens**. The uniform corpus,
whose non-realizable rows spread over depths 12–25, sits at 90.5% and shows
no further decline (its per-depth counts are single- and double-digit, so
only the pooled figure is meaningful). Reading the two together: the
catalogue-wide closure fraction is **about 90%**, and the prefix's 91.1% is
at most a percentage point optimistic.

### 4.3 The residue bias — this is the one caveat that matters

The denominators above are *certified* non-realizable classes. Classes the
sweep could neither realize nor refute (RESIDUE / OPEN) are excluded, and
they are **not** excluded at random:

> **Proposition R.** If some deletion χ∖e of a uniform rank-4 chirotope on 9
> elements is non-realizable, then χ has a biquadratic final polynomial.
>
> *Proof.* χ∖e is a uniform rank-4 class on 8 elements, and that cell is
> completely classified: `certs_4_8.jsonl` settles all 2,628 classes, 2,604
> by an explicit integer matrix and 24 by a Gordan vector, and `checkcert.py`
> accepts every one. So χ∖e is one of those 24 and its class carries a
> Gordan vector. Existence of a biquadratic final polynomial is an invariant
> of the G'-class (§5.1), so χ∖e itself has one. Lift it along the
> order-preserving relabelling (§5) and it is a Gordan vector for χ. ∎

So a class with an inherited obstruction is essentially never left OPEN, and
the OPEN set is enriched in exactly the minor-minimal population. Measured:

| corpus | OPEN rows | OPEN rows with a non-realizable deletion |
|---|---|---|
| sweep prefix | 60 | **0** |
| uniform sample | 391 | **0** |

**451 of 451**, with zero exceptions. (`SCOPING.md` §6.3 reported the same
on 18 and on 33 classes; this is ~9× more.) Two consequences:

* the closure fraction **91.1% is an upper bound** and the minor-minimal
  count **1,279 is a lower bound**, both by the same mechanism. The uniform
  corpus's residue is 7.2% of it — the same order as the 8.9% minimal rate —
  so the bias is not negligible, though the sweep's own cascade is much
  stronger than the pilots' (60 open in 1,445,227 rows, 0.004%) and its
  prefix is correspondingly less exposed;
* Proposition R **sharpens the conjecture** at the end of
  `WALK_THEORY.md` §7. That conjecture reads *"a uniform rank-4 OM on 9
  elements all of whose 8-element deletions are realizable, and which has no
  biquadratic final polynomial, is realizable."* Proposition R says the
  first hypothesis follows from the second, so the conjecture is **equivalent
  to** the shorter *"a uniform rank-4 OM on 9 elements with no biquadratic
  final polynomial is realizable"* — the deletion clause looked like an
  independent hypothesis and is not one.

The flip side, stated plainly: **the minor test settles none of the sweep's
open classes.** That was the one place a concrete operational payoff could
have appeared, and it is empty for a structural reason, not by accident.

### 4.4 Calibration one rank down, where the answer is published

The identical question at (3,10) has a published ground truth and a
one-element obstruction set: (3,9) has exactly one non-realizable class (the
non-Pappus configuration) and (3,10) has exactly 242, reproduced
independently in `SCOPING.md` §4.1.

| | |
|---|---|
| (3,10) non-realizable classes | 242 (all inputs verified to be distinct canonical keys) |
| with the non-Pappus (3,9) class as a deletion | **183** |
| closure fraction | **75.62%**, 95% CI [69.84%, 80.60%] |
| minor-minimal at (3,10) | **59** |
| with a non-realizable contraction | 0 (rank 2, one class per n, realizable) |

So the closure fraction is not a universal constant: 76% against one
excluded minor at rank 3, ~90% against twenty-four at rank 4. Both are
"most, but a fixed fraction escapes". The escaping fraction — 24% and 9% —
is the rate at which genuinely new obstructions appear per element added,
and it does not look like it is going to zero.

## 5. Direction (⇐), made concrete: the certificate lifts

Lemma D proves that a class with a non-realizable deletion is
non-realizable. `liftcert.py` turns that proof into a certificate object
that the independent checker accepts.

Let φ: E∖{e} → {1..8} be the order-preserving bijection and δ = χ∖e. A
biquadratic final polynomial for δ is a list of weighted strict
inequalities, each naming a three-term GP relation (L; a,b,c,d) of δ, which
of its three terms is the BIG one, and a positive integer weight, such that
Σ wᵢ vᵢ = 0 with vᵢ = e_p + e_q − e_s − e_t. Apply φ⁻¹ to L and to
(a,b,c,d). Because φ⁻¹ is strictly increasing:

* (φ⁻¹L; φ⁻¹a < φ⁻¹b < φ⁻¹c < φ⁻¹d) is a genuine three-term GP relation of
  χ, already in normal form;
* each of its three signed terms **equals** the corresponding term of the
  δ-relation — the two brackets are equal by the definition of deletion, and
  the tuple-sorting signs are unchanged because an increasing map creates no
  inversions. So the same term is the odd one out: `big` and `small` carry
  over verbatim;
* B ↦ φ⁻¹B is injective from the 70 bases of δ into the 126 bases of χ, so
  the weighted combination still cancels coordinate by coordinate.

The lift is therefore a **pure relabelling of indices** — no group element,
no LP, no arithmetic.

**Verified.** 40 sampled classes with a non-realizable deletion: the
8-element Gordan vector was recomputed from scratch, lifted, and both the
8-element and the 9-element records were handed to `checkcert.py`. **80/80
accepted.** Five deliberate sabotages of the same lift — lifted with the
wrong deleted element, one weight altered, `big`/`small` swapped, a term
dropped, the certificate attached to a different 9-element class — were
**5/5 rejected**, each with a specific diagnosis (`data/lifted_canaries.jsonl`).

### 5.1 Why BFP-existence is a class invariant (needed by Proposition R)

Write the GP relation for (L; a,b,c,d) as the alternating expression
T₁ = χ(L,a,b)χ(L,c,d), T₂ = −χ(L,a,c)χ(L,b,d), T₃ = χ(L,a,d)χ(L,b,c).

* Transposing two of a,b,c,d permutes (T₁,T₂,T₃) among themselves and
  multiplies all three by −1 (check: swapping c,d gives (−T₁,−T₃,−T₂);
  swapping b,c gives (−T₂,−T₁,−T₃)). So any reordering acts by a permutation
  of the three term indices together with **one common sign**.
* Transposing the two elements of L multiplies each bracket by −1, hence
  each term by +1.
* Reorienting a set ε multiplies every term by (−1)^{|ε ∩ {a,b,c,d}|}
  (the L-part appears in both brackets of every term and cancels) — again
  **common**.
* The global sign multiplies each term by (−1)² = +1.

A common sign and a permutation of the three indices do not change *which*
term is the odd one out; they only rename it. Since relabelling also
permutes the C(n,r) basis coordinates bijectively, a Gordan vector maps to a
Gordan vector. Hence a class has a biquadratic final polynomial or none of
its representatives does. Empirically: 25/25 deletions identified as one of
the 24 — arbitrary labelled representatives, not catalog reps — yielded a
Gordan vector from a fresh LP, all accepted by `checkcert.py` (canary C2).

## 6. The minor-minimal residue at n = 9

**1,279 classes** in the frozen prefix, listed by canonical key in
`data/minimal_sweep.txt`; their full certificates are in
`data/certs_minimal_sweep.jsonl` and **all 1,279 were accepted by
`checkcert.py`**. Each has all nine deletions realizable and all nine
contractions realizable, so by Lemma M every proper minor is realizable:
each is a genuine new excluded minor for realizability at n = 9.

They are **8.88%** of the certified non-realizable classes in the prefix —
matching, at 570× the sample size, the 2-of-25 (8%) that `SCOPING.md` §6.3
reported from a hand sample.

### 6.1 The list survives a falsification test that bypasses the pipeline

A class lands on this list because all nine of its deletions were
*identified*, by canonicalization, as realizable (4,8) classes. That
identification is the one step whose failure would silently inflate the
list. `verify_minimal.py` tests the claim without canonicalizing anything:

> A realizable oriented matroid provably has **no** Gordan vector — the logs
> of its brackets satisfy every strict inequality. So a single biquadratic
> final polynomial found among the deletions of a minor-minimal class
> refutes the list. Conversely each of the 24 obstructions has one, and
> BFP-existence is a class invariant (§5.1), so the test is sharp both ways.

| | |
|---|---|
| deletions of the 1,279 minimal classes | 11,511 (11,286 distinct labelled) |
| put through a fresh BFP search | all of them, 14 ms each, 154 s at 2 workers |
| **Gordan vectors found** | **0** |
| positive control: deletions identified as one of the 24 | **60/60** produced a Gordan vector |

Zero hits over 11,286 independent LPs, against a positive control that fires
60 times out of 60. The minimal list does not depend on the canonicalizer
being right.

**Extrapolation, clearly labelled as one.** `SCOPING.md` §6.2 measures the
catalogue-wide non-realizable density at 2.10% [1.64%, 2.68%] on a uniform
sample, i.e. ≈194,700 [152,500, 248,200] non-realizable classes. At an 8.9%
minimal rate that is **≈17,000 minor-minimal classes at n = 9**, order
10^4, and the residue bias of §4.3 pushes it up rather than down. Two
independent sources of error compound here (the density and the rate), so
treat this as an order of magnitude, not a figure.

An excluded-minor list of 10^4 entries is a lookup table, not a theorem.

---

## 7. Structure of the minimal set — a negative finding

The question was whether the minimal set is a transportable template family,
in the way `ai/maxout`'s single-class certificates were. Comparing the 1,279
minor-minimal classes against a matched random sample of 1,279
non-realizable classes that *do* have a witness:

| | minor-minimal | has a witness |
|---|---|---|
| tree depth (mean, range) | 15.2 [11, 16] | 15.0 [7, 16] |
| mutable bases (mean, range) | 14.5 [9, 20] | 15.0 [9, 21] |
| &#124;Stab&#124; histogram | 2:1272, 4:5, 6:1, 12:1 | 2:1273, 4:6 |
| all nine deletions in distinct (4,8) classes | 1003 (78.4%) | 903 (70.6%) |
| BFP support (terms), mean / median / range | **73.5** / 74 / [41, 96] | **61.7** / 62 / [27, 96] |
| BFP total weight, mean | **249,833** | 106,676 |

* **Depth, mutable-basis count and stabilizer do not separate the two
  populations.** The stabilizer is the minimum possible, order 2, for
  1,272/1,279 minimal classes — they are as generic as anything else in the
  catalog. This reproduces, on the minor question, the same conclusion
  `WALK_THEORY.md` §5 reached on the difficulty question.
* **Every one of the 1,279 minimal classes has a distinct nine-element
  deletion multiset**, and between them they use 1,347 different realizable
  (4,8) classes as deletions. There is no small family of "near-miss"
  8-element configurations that they all sit above.
* **The one thing that does separate them is certificate size.** Minimal
  classes need a Gordan vector with ~19% more terms and ~2.3× the total
  weight. This **replicates independently in the uniform corpus** (75.6 vs
  62.9 terms), which matters: it is not an artifact of the depth-ordered
  prefix.

The contrast with n = 8 is the most interesting structural fact found:

| | the 24 excluded minors at n = 8 | the 1,279 minimal classes at n = 9 |
|---|---|---|
| symmetry | 21 of 24 have a non-trivial relabelling stabilizer; 9 of 24 are *colour-blind* (the canonical convention's refinement fails to distinguish any two ground elements, so all 8! relabellings are admissible — against 1,819 of 2,628 catalog rows having a single admissible relabelling) | 1,272 of 1,279 have &#124;Stab&#124; = 2, the minimum |
| mutable bases, against the mean of their own cell | 10.9 vs 11.7 — **below** | 14.5 vs 14.7 (`WALK_THEORY` §5) — **at** the mean |
| how many are there | 24 | order 10^4 |

The 24 are special, highly symmetric configurations of the kind that get
names. The new obstructions at n = 9 are generic and numerous. **There is no
visible transportable template.** That is the finding; it is negative, and
it is why §3's theorem cannot be made to carry weight.

---

## 8. The payoff arithmetic, honestly

**All timings below were taken while the 4-worker sweep was running.** The
same contention inflates them all: `liftcert.py` measures a (9,4)
biquadratic final polynomial at 599 ms where `SCOPING.md` §6.1 measures
~250 ms uncontended, a factor of 2.4. Ratios between contended numbers are
meaningful; mixing them with uncontended figures is not, and where that is
unavoidable it is flagged.

### 8.1 The minor test as a production filter

`fastminor.py` implements the exact two-stage test:

* **Stage 1**, vectorized: from the mutable-basis mask of all nine deletions
  compute deg(i), m2(i,j) and comp(i) = (deg(i), sorted multiset over j≠i of
  (m2(i,j), deg(j))); the triple (#mutable, sorted deg, sorted comp) is a
  G'-invariant. The 24 obstructions take 19 distinct values of it. Anything
  else is *proved* not to be one of the 24, with no canonicalization.
* **Stage 2**: canonicalize the survivors and test the key.

Stage 1 can only produce false positives, so the composition is exact —
confirmed on 2,000 rows against the full pipeline, **0 disagreements**.

| workload | ms/class | stage-2 survivors |
|---|---|---|
| realistic population (80% realizable) | **6.07** | 73 / 18,000 = 0.41% |
| non-realizable-heavy | 187.9 | 2,222 / 18,000 = 12.3% |

(The refinement matters: without `comp` the survivor rate is 33% and the
population workload costs 12.4 ms/class. Without stage 1 at all — nine full
canonicalizations — it is ~83 ms/class.)

### 8.2 What fraction of the sweep's BFP searches was avoidable

BFP fires in `sweep49.py` only when the wall crossing fails. In the frozen
prefix that is at most 14,396 + 60 + 575 = 15,031 of 1,445,227 classes,
**≤1.04%**. Of the certified non-realizable ones, 91.1% would have been
answered by the minor test instead. So:

> **fraction of all (4,9) classes whose BFP search a minor test could have
> replaced: ≈0.91%.**

### 8.3 Would minor-test-first pay?

**As a universal pre-filter: no, it loses.** 9,276,595 classes × 6.07 ms =
**15.6 core-hours** spent, to save 0.91% × 9,276,595 × 250 ms = **5.9
core-hours** of LP (using the uncontended BFP figure, which is generous to
the filter). Net loss ≈10 core-hours against a walk that costs ~70
core-hours in total. Even at zero filter cost the ceiling on the saving is
under 10% of the sweep.

**As a replacement for BFP on the crossing-failure slice: marginal.** On
that slice the minor test costs 187.9 ms (contended) against a BFP at 599 ms
(contended) — about 3× cheaper — but the slice is 1% of the sweep, so the
whole saving is ~0.5% of total runtime, and 8.9% of the slice still needs
the LP.

**Conclusion: minor filtering buys essentially nothing in compute at (4,9).**
Its value is that it is a *second, independent* decision path (a Gordan
vector obtained by index remapping rather than by an LP), that it produces
the closure measurement, and that it yields Proposition R.

---

## 9. Does this make (4,10) conceivable?

**No, and the reason is enumeration, not decision.**

**Size of the cell.** Uniform rank-4 class counts: (4,6) 1, (4,7) 11, (4,8)
2,628, (4,9) 9,276,595 — successive ratios 11, 239, 3,530, i.e. the ratio
itself grows by 15–22× per element added. Equivalently log₂(count) goes
3.46 → 11.36 → 23.14, with second differences +7.90 → +11.78. Extrapolating
either way gives a next ratio of 3×10⁴–8×10⁴ and

> **(4,10) ≈ a few × 10^11 classes** (take 10^11–10^12 as the honest band;
> this is a one-step extrapolation and nothing more).

Rank 3 behaves the same way one step earlier — 4, 11, 135, 4,382, 312,356
with ratios 2.75, 12.3, 32.5, 71.3 — and there the ratio-of-ratios decays
towards ~2, so the rank-4 figure may be on the high side.

**What that costs before any realizability question is asked**, at 5×10^11
classes:

| | (4,9), actual | (4,10), projected |
|---|---|---|
| classes | 9,276,595 | ~5×10^11 |
| traversal at the walk's 26.5 ms/class | 68 core-hours | **3.7×10^6 core-hours** (~420 core-years) |
| canonical keys at 16 B/class | 148 MB | **8 TB** |
| the compact tree certificate (1.12 B/class, measured on `tree_4_9.npz`) | 10.4 MB | 560 GB |
| the sweep's realization store (`Z.dat`, 4·n·4 B/class) | 1.34 GB | **80 TB** |

So the blocker is not exotic — it is a multi-hundred-core-year traversal, a
sort-merge dedup over 8 TB of keys, and 80 TB of realizations if the
parent-crossing walk is used at all. The (4,9) cell closed on a laptop
overnight at ~86 core-hours; n = 10 is 4–5 orders of magnitude beyond that.
And **no filter helps with the part that is expensive**: a filter decides
classes, it does not help you enumerate them. Applied as a universal
pre-filter the minor test would itself cost 5×10^11 × ~4 ms ≈ 5.6×10^5
core-hours — 15% of the traversal, for a saving bounded by the ~1% of
classes that reach an LP.

**What the minor test does make affordable at n = 10.** Deciding an
*individual* (4,10) class. Its ten deletions are (4,9) classes, and the
machinery costs, measured here:

| operation, measured on 60 classes of each population | cost per chirotope |
|---|---|
| the refined G'-invariant of a (4,9) chirotope | 0.12 – 0.23 ms |
| full canonicalization of a (4,9) chirotope | 0.13 ms (population) · 0.20 ms (non-realizable) · 2.74 ms (minor-minimal) |
| ⇒ minor test for one (4,10) class, ten deletions | **≈2–6 ms** |

Note that (4,9) chirotopes canonicalize 20–400× faster than (4,8) ones: the
colour refinement almost always splits the ground set at n = 9, whereas the
non-realizable (4,8) classes are unusually colour-blind (§7). The n = 10
minor test also needs a membership structure over the (4,9) non-realizable
set (≈2×10^5 classes, ≈3 MB of keys) — which the running sweep is producing.
At an ~90% hit rate that decides most non-realizable (4,10) classes in a few
milliseconds, with a certificate obtained by index remapping.

That supports a **sampling** study rather than a sweep: draw (4,10) classes
as single-element extensions of already-realized (4,9) classes and decide
each — minor test first, then a wall crossing warm-started from the parent's
realization, then BFP. For 10^6 samples that is ~1 core-hour of filtering,
~15–25 core-hours of crossings (guessing 2–3× the (4,9) walk's measured
26.5 ms/class for the larger matrix and basis set — this factor is *not*
measured), and a few core-hours of LP on the failures: **an overnight run
again**, enough to measure the (4,10) non-realizable density and the (4,10)
closure fraction to two or three digits.

**Caveat that must travel with any such result:** extension-sampling is not
uniform on (4,10) classes — a class with more (4,9) parents is oversampled —
so it estimates an extension-weighted density, not the catalogue density,
unless the weighting is corrected by the parent counts.

---

## 10. Canaries and trust boundary

`python canaries.py --tag sweep --all` — all pass.

**Sabotage (must be caught).**

| | result |
|---|---|
| S1 two entries of the deletion index table swapped | GP validity of the deletions drops from 1080/1080 to 1030/1080 → caught |
| S2 one sign of the contraction table flipped | 1080/1080 → 977/1080 → caught |
| S3 one corrupted sign in the 9-element class | 225/225 deletions behave exactly as required: unchanged iff the corrupted basis contains the deleted element, changed otherwise |
| S4 200 random sign strings | 0/200 pass the GP conditions; 0/20 of their meaningless keys land in `cat_4_8` |
| lifted certificate: wrong element / bad weight / big↔small / dropped term / wrong class | 5/5 **rejected** by `checkcert.py`, each with a specific reason |

**Confirmation (a second route must agree).**

| | result |
|---|---|
| C1 no REALIZABLE class has a non-realizable minor (Lemmas D + C) | **5,608 realizable rows, 0 violations** |
| C2 deletions identified as one of the 24: run BFP directly on the deletion | 25/25 got a Gordan vector; `checkcert.py` accepted all |
| C3 deletions identified as realizable: realize the deletion directly | 25/25 realized; `checkcert.py` accepted all |
| C4 brute-force canonicalization over the **whole** group (8!·2⁸·2 elements; `bfcanon.py`, no shared code, no colour refinement, no sign lattice) | 12/12 land in the class the pipeline assigned, 12/12 separated from a random other class |
| C5 (`verify_minimal.py`) every deletion of every minor-minimal class through a fresh BFP search — canonicalization not used | **0 Gordan vectors in 11,286 LPs**; positive control 60/60 |

**Global checks, asserted on every row rather than sampled** (`minorsweep.py`):

* **G1** all 185,139 deletions and 185,139 contractions of the (4,9) corpora
  — plus the 2,420 + 2,420 at (3,10) — are valid uniform chirotopes;
* **G2** every canonical key produced lands inside the corresponding
  complete catalog (2,628 / 135 / 4,382 rows) — 0 misses;
* **G3** no REALIZABLE input row has a non-realizable minor.

**Independence.** `bfcanon.py` was validated by exhaustively enumerating all
2^20 sign vectors at (3,6), keeping the 23,808 valid chirotopes, and
partitioning them by brute-force group orbit: it finds **exactly 4 classes**,
the published count. The catalog reps themselves are literal fixed points of
the canonicalizer (checked for all 2,628 (4,8) rows, all 135 (3,8) rows, all
4,382 (3,9) rows, and the 242 (3,10) inputs).

**What is still delegated.** Canonicalization in the main pipeline is
`ai/omgamma/coverage_checker.py` — the standalone checker, which shares no
code with omgamma's generator side and is the same decoder `ai/omreal`
already used, so the (4,8) catalog keys, the sweep's (4,9) keys and the keys
here are in one convention by construction. The realizability verdicts are
`ai/omreal`'s and are re-checked by `checkcert.py`. Nothing here depends on
`WALK_THEORY.md`'s Corollary B or on Roudneff–Sturmfels.

Two things *do* depend on omgamma beyond the decoder, and only one of them
is load-bearing. The **completeness** of the (4,8), (3,8) and (3,9) catalogs
— 2,628 / 135 / 4,382 classes, which is what makes "identified against the
catalog" a total function and makes G2 a real check — rests on omgamma's
mass identity and on agreement with the published counts. The
**completeness of the (4,9) catalog** (9,276,595) is used only for the
catalogue-wide extrapolations in §6 and §9; every measured fraction is over
classes actually certified and would survive a revision of that count.

**Not touched:** `ai/omreal/` is read-only throughout. The shards were read
with a reader that consumes only complete lines and records byte offsets.

| `data/report_sweep.json`, `data/report_uniform.json`, `data/rank3check.json`, `data/fastminor.json`, `data/verify_minimal.json` | machine-readable results (tracked) |

Large regenerable artifacts are gitignored (`data/harvest_*.jsonl`,
`data/minors_*.jsonl`, `data/certs_minimal_*.jsonl`, the identification
caches). The regeneration order is in `.gitignore`; running it end to end on
the frozen prefix costs about 25 minutes at 2 workers, most of it the
(4,8) canonicalizations, which the cache then makes free. To rebuild the
minimal-set certificate file:

```python
mini = {json.loads(l)['chi'] for l in open('data/minors_sweep.jsonl')
        if json.loads(l)['verdict'] == 'NON_REALIZABLE'
        and not json.loads(l)['del_nonreal']}
# then filter data/harvest_sweep.jsonl to those chi and run
# python ../omreal/checkcert.py on the result
```

## 12. What would change the verdict

1. **The sweep finishing.** It would settle the closure fraction over all
   9,276,595 classes and make the minimal list complete rather than a
   prefix. `harvest.py --extend` then `minorsweep.py --extend` does it; the
   identification cache means the marginal cost is only the new 8-element
   minors.
2. **Structure inside the 1,279.** Nothing found here separates them from
   generic non-realizable classes except certificate size. A property that
   did — a common submatroid, a common extension pattern, a bound on the
   Gordan support — would turn the list into a theorem. This is the open
   question the negative finding in §7 leaves.
3. **Proposition R applied to the residue.** It says the sweep's OPEN set
   consists only of hard-but-realizable classes and BFP-resistant
   minor-minimal ones. If the sweep terminates with a non-empty OPEN set,
   every member is a candidate for a **BFP-resistant uniform oriented
   matroid at n = 9** — which `WALK_THEORY.md` §7 already identifies as a
   better result than the count. §4.3 narrows where to look.
